- ✗ **D. Enforce PB first:** a project can be in only one enforced configuration, and enforcing the move first would risk real denials before any test.

## Key idea
Test a project move with dry run, respecting one enforced and one dry run membership, and keep the real protection until you enforce.
Q010763:
## Firewalls across VPC Network Peering
Peering gives two VPC networks private connectivity, but each network keeps its own security.
- Peering does **not exchange firewall rules or policies**. Each side needs its own ingress allow rules, because implied deny ingress applies.
- Network tags and service-account targets in VPC firewall rules resolve only to instances in the rule's own network, so a tag from the peer cannot be a source.
- Secure tags in a network firewall policy are different: used as a **source**, a secure tag can identify instances in the tag's own network and in networks peered with it. Used as a target, it applies only inside the network the tag is scoped to.
- Implied allow egress means no egress rule is needed unless an egress deny exists.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Port not carried:** peering carries all protocols and ports for private addresses, and the issue is the source match, not the port.
- ✓ **B. IP-range or secure-tag source (correct):** the rule must name the peer subnet's address range, or use a secure tag in a network firewall policy, because a network tag never matches VMs of the peer.
- ✗ **C. Peering exchanges firewall rules:** it does not; firewall rules and policies stay local to each network.
- ✗ **D. Egress deny:** the implied rule for egress is allow, so no egress rule is needed in net-app.

## Key idea
Firewall rules do not span peering; match peer sources by IP range or by secure tag, never by network tag.
Q010764:
## Controlling who may peer
Peering is established by network admins at both ends, with no central approval by default: **by default a network admin for one network can peer with any other network**. The Restrict VPC peering usage constraint (`constraints/compute.restrictVpcPeering`) is a list constraint that defines which VPC networks may be peered with the networks of a project, folder or organization. Values use forms such as `under:organizations/ORG_ID`, `under:folders/FOLDER_ID` or a single network path.
- It is **preventive**: creation of peering with a non-allowed network fails.
- It complements, but does not replace, firewall rules, which still decide what traffic is accepted.
- Audit-log alerts are detective, so the peering already exists when someone reviews it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. VPC Service Controls:** perimeters protect Google API data, and they do not govern VPC peering between networks.
- ✗ **B. Deny RFC 1918 ingress:** that would also break normal internal traffic, and it does not stop the peering, only part of its traffic.
- ✓ **C. Peering restriction constraint (correct):** it denies peering to networks outside the allowed organization before the connection exists.
- ✗ **D. Audit-log alert:** the peering would already be live between detection and removal, so this is detective rather than preventive.

## Key idea
Use the VPC peering restriction constraint to prevent peering with networks outside the approved set.
Q010765:
## Implied firewall rules still apply across peering
Every VPC network has two implied rules: allow all egress and deny all ingress, at the lowest priority. With peering:
- Traffic into a network must be allowed by that network's own ingress rules, with sources that may include the peer's subnet ranges.
- Egress to the peer needs no rule unless the network has egress deny rules.
- Peered networks do not exchange or merge firewall rules.
## Applying it here
Only the database network must open the port, restricted to the application subnet. Anything more is unneeded permission.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Explicit egress rule too:** implied allow egress already lets net-app send to the peer, so the second rule adds nothing.
- ✗ **B. Cross-network tags:** network tags do not resolve across peering, so those rules would match nothing.
- ✓ **C. Single ingress rule on the database side (correct):** implied deny ingress protects the database by default, and a rule with the source range admits only the application subnet.
- ✗ **D. Egress only:** ingress to net-db would remain denied by the implied rule, so connections would fail.

## Key idea
Across peering, open ingress on the destination network to the source ranges; implied allow egress covers the rest.
Q010766:
## VMs as routers
By default a Compute Engine VM sends and receives only packets that carry its own address. When **IP forwarding** (`canIpForward`) is enabled on the VM, it can also relay packets for other addresses. That is what network virtual appliances need, and also what an attacker needs to build a hidden path between tiers.
- The Restrict VM IP forwarding constraint (`constraints/compute.managed.vmCanIpForward`; the legacy `constraints/compute.vmCanIpForward` is still listed) denies creating or updating VMs with IP forwarding enabled. By default any VM may enable it.
- Exceptions are made by setting a different policy on the appliance project, or by marking instances with tags and using conditional rules.
- Firewall rules match addresses, ports and protocols of the packet; they do not know whether a VM is acting as a relay.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. External IP restriction:** forwarding works between internal addresses, so a VM without a public address can still relay traffic.
- ✗ **B. Destination-address firewall rule:** firewall rules cannot express "not this VM's own address", and a relay VM would still forward packets that the rule allows.
- ✗ **C. VPC Service Controls:** perimeters govern Google API requests, not packets that VMs relay between VPC networks or subnets.
- ✓ **D. IP forwarding constraint with an appliance-project override (correct):** the control that creates relay-capable VMs is switched off for the folder, and only the approved appliances keep the capability.

## Key idea
Restrict VM IP forwarding by organization policy, and exempt only approved appliance projects.
Q010767:
## Roles in a Shared VPC
- **Shared VPC Admin** (`compute.xpnAdmin` plus Project IAM Admin) enables host projects and attaches service projects, at organization or folder scope.
- **Network Admin** (`compute.networkAdmin`) on the host project has full control over network resources **except** firewall rules and SSL certificates.
- **Security Admin** (`compute.securityAdmin`) on the host project manages firewall rules and SSL certificates.
- **Service Project Admins** hold `compute.networkUser` on selected subnets (or the whole host project) and create and manage instances in their service projects, without being able to change the shared network.
This split lets the organization enforce consistent network control while delegating compute administration.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Shared VPC Admin creates firewall rules:** Shared VPC Admin attaches and enables projects; it is not the firewall management role.
- ✓ **B. Security Admin (correct):** the role is the intended grant for managing firewall rules and SSL certificates, which keeps them apart from routing and subnet administration.
- ✗ **C. Network Admin includes firewall rules:** Network Admin has full control over network resources except firewall rules and SSL certificates.
- ✗ **D. Network Admin for service teams:** service project teams only use shared subnets through Compute Network User, and Network Admin would let them change the shared network.

## Key idea
Split Shared VPC duties: Shared VPC Admin attaches projects, Network Admin manages routing and subnets, Security Admin manages firewall rules.
Q010768:
## Rule actions in firewall policies
Hierarchical firewall policies are evaluated from the organization down to folders, before VPC firewall rules and network firewall policies. A rule's action decides what happens next:
- `allow`: permit the traffic and **stop evaluating**, so lower levels cannot block it.
- `deny`: drop the traffic and stop evaluating, so lower levels cannot allow it.
- `goto_next`: stop evaluating this policy and continue with the next step in the evaluation order, which lets a lower level decide.
- `apply_security_profile_group`: send the traffic to Cloud NGFW Enterprise for inspection.
## Applying it here
Telnet must be absolutely blocked, so it takes a deny at the top. SSH is delegated downward, which is what goto_next expresses. An allow at the top would take the decision away from the projects.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Deny plus goto_next (correct):** the deny cannot be overridden below, and goto_next hands SSH to the next evaluation step, where project rules decide.
- ✗ **B. Allow SSH:** allow ends evaluation, so project teams could no longer block SSH with their own rules.
- ✗ **C. Deny both:** a deny at the top cannot be overridden by lower-level allow rules.
- ✗ **D. goto_next for Telnet:** Telnet would depend on lower-level rules and could be allowed by a project; the allow rule for SSH also removes the delegation.

## Key idea
Use deny for non-negotiable blocks and goto_next to delegate a decision to lower levels.
Q010769:
## Context-aware access to a perimeter
An **access level** in Access Context Manager describes requirements for a request. Conditions can test the IP range, region, user or service account identity, and the **device policy** attribute.
- Device information comes from **Endpoint Verification**. Criteria include screen lock enabled, storage encryption enabled, and an operating system kind and version.
- An access level can be attached to the perimeter, or used as a `source` in an ingress rule, which can also limit identities, services and methods.
- Conditions in one level are combined, so a request must satisfy IP, identity and device attributes together if they are all listed.
## Applying it here
Address ranges change and do not describe the device, so the device policy is the stable signal, and the ingress rule keeps access limited to the analyst group and BigQuery.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Device-policy access level in an ingress rule (correct):** it admits only requests from devices that meet the baseline, from any network, and only for the analyst group and the chosen service.
- ✗ **B. Dry run:** dry run only logs what a configuration would block; it never refuses requests, and it has no device-checking function.
- ✗ **C. IP-range access level:** the addresses change often, so the list is always stale, and it says nothing about the state of the device that uses them.
- ✗ **D. Egress rule:** egress covers calls that leave the perimeter, whereas analysts connecting from outside make requests that enter it.

## Key idea
Use a device-policy access level, as the source of an ingress rule, when device state rather than network location should admit a request.
Q010770:
## Network controls do not see API-level destinations
A firewall decides on IP addresses, ports and protocols (and, with Cloud NGFW, FQDNs). When the data VM talks to `storage.googleapis.com`, the destination is the same shared Google API endpoint for **every** bucket, including the attacker's.
- Data encapsulation therefore needs a control that understands which project owns the resource being accessed. VPC Service Controls checks the projects involved in each API call and blocks calls that cross the perimeter, for example copying to a bucket outside it.
- Exceptions are explicit egress rules naming the identities, methods and external projects.
- Combine with the restricted VIP so that only supported APIs are reachable from the network, and keep IAM least privilege and CMEK as further layers.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Stricter application ingress:** the exfiltration runs outbound from the compromised data VM, so ingress tightening does not close the path.
- ✓ **B. Perimeter around the data projects (correct):** it denies service operations that copy data to resources outside the perimeter, which firewall rules cannot distinguish.
- ✗ **C. Hostname allow rule:** the hostname is common to every bucket, so a rule on it still allows the attacker's destination.
- ✗ **D. Bucket names in firewall rules:** firewall rules do not inspect API request content, so they cannot match bucket names.

## Key idea
Firewalls cannot tell which bucket an API call targets; use a VPC Service Controls perimeter to encapsulate data at the API level.
Q010771:
## VPC properties that matter for security
- A VPC network is a global resource, and subnets are regional. Networks created in **auto mode** get a subnet per region with predefined ranges; **custom mode** lets you define only the subnets and ranges you need, which avoids unplanned overlap with peered or on-premises ranges.
- The organization policy constraint `constraints/compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation` prevents new projects from getting a default network with its permissive default rules.
- Every network has implied deny ingress and allow egress. Rules should be explicit.
## N-tier isolation
Isolation between web, application and database tiers comes from allow rules that match the tier, not broad ranges: reference service accounts or secure tags, so rules follow workloads rather than IP addresses.
- web to app on the app port, app to database on the database port, everything else denied.
- No tier other than the app tier should reach the database.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Database port from the internet:** this opens the data tier to the whole internet.
- ✗ **B. One broad internal rule:** this lets a compromised web VM reach every other tier, which defeats isolation.
- ✓ **C. Skip default network, custom mode (correct):** it removes the preconfigured network and its permissive rules, and gives control of the address plan.
- ✗ **D. One shared subnet and OS firewalls:** this makes isolation depend on settings inside each VM, which a compromised VM can change.
- ✓ **E. Identity-based tier rules (correct):** allow rules between adjacent tiers only keep a compromised web VM from reaching the database directly.

## Key idea
Remove the default network, use custom mode, and allow only adjacent-tier traffic by service account or secure tag.
Q010772:
## How Cloud EKM works
With Cloud EKM the key material is created and kept in a supported external key manager (Fortanix, Futurex or Thales). A Cloud EKM key version holds only a reference (key URI or key path) plus extra internal key material that stays in Cloud KMS. For every cryptographic operation, Cloud EKM sends a request to the external manager, which wraps or unwraps a layer of encryption using the external key.
## Internet versus VPC
- `EXTERNAL`: Cloud EKM reaches the manager over the internet. It works in most locations, including multi-regions, but the path can add latency and failures.
- `EXTERNAL_VPC`: Cloud EKM reaches the manager over a Virtual Private Cloud network. The documentation positions it for better availability, so the keys and the resources they protect are less likely to become unavailable. It is available in most regional locations but not in multi-regional ones.
When the external key is unreachable, Cloud KMS returns `FAILED_PRECONDITION`, and the protected resource cannot be used until the key answers again.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cloud HSM in a multi-region:** this moves the key material into Google-managed hardware, which breaks the requirement to keep the key in the bank's external key manager.
- ✗ **B. Global location:** `global` is one of the locations where Cloud EKM keys cannot be created, and a location name does not decide how close a partner is.
- ✗ **C. Caching key material:** Cloud EKM never caches or stores the external key material in Google Cloud; each request goes to the external manager, so there is nothing to cache.
- ✓ **D. Cloud EKM over a VPC (correct):** it keeps the key material in the external manager, as policy demands, and replaces the internet path with a private network path that improves availability. The single-region data fits because this option exists in regional locations.

## Key idea
Cloud EKM over a VPC gives better availability than the internet path while keeping key material outside Google, but only in regional locations.
Q010773:
## Manually managed versus coordinated external keys
- A **manually managed** external key is created in the external manager first, then referenced in Cloud KMS by URI or path. Rotation and destruction must be done in both systems by hand, and automatic rotation is not supported.
- A **coordinated** external key is created from Cloud KMS through an EKM connection over a VPC with "EKM key management from Cloud KMS" enabled. This needs an external key manager partner that supports the Cloud EKM control plane. Cloud EKM then asks the external manager to create, rotate and destroy key material, so a symmetric key can rotate on a schedule.
## Why it matters to a security engineer
Many standards require regular rotation. If the key must stay outside Google, the control plane decides whether rotation can be a schedule or a manual runbook.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Period above 365 days:** no such minimum exists; the schedule fails because the key is manually managed, not because of the period chosen.
- ✓ **B. Coordinated external key (correct):** the documentation states that automatic rotation is not supported for manually managed external keys, while coordinated keys over a VPC can rotate symmetric keys on a set schedule because Cloud EKM coordinates the new material with the external manager.
- ✗ **C. Software keys only:** automatic rotation also works for Cloud HSM keys and coordinated external keys; switching to software would give up the requirement for external custody.
- ✗ **D. Support rotation:** rotation is a customer operation in Cloud KMS and in the external manager; Google Support does not rotate keys on request.

## Key idea
Scheduled rotation of external keys needs coordinated keys (EKM over a VPC with Cloud KMS key management and a supporting partner); manually managed ones rotate by runbook.
Q010774:
## What Cloud EKM promises and what it costs
Cloud EKM gives key provenance (you decide where keys live), access control (the Google Cloud project can use a key only while the external manager allows it, and you can revoke that at any time), and central management of keys across cloud and on-premises data.
The price of that control is dependency. Google has no control over the availability of the external key, and cannot recover data if keys managed outside Google Cloud are lost.
## Practical consequences
- Every operation goes to the partner, so partner downtime becomes outage of the protected resource.
- You need a support contract with the partner; Google Cloud support covers Google Cloud services only.
- Some locations, including `global`, are not available for Cloud EKM.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Never cached (correct):** the external key material stays in the external manager and Cloud EKM contacts it for each request, so an unreachable key produces failures instead of a fallback.
- ✗ **B. Global location:** `global` and `nam-eur-asia1` are not available for Cloud EKM.
- ✗ **C. Backup copy:** Cloud KMS holds only extra internal key material used as a layer of encryption, and the data cannot be decrypted without the external key.
- ✗ **D. Support:** Google Cloud support helps only with Google Cloud services; a support contract with the external key management partner is needed for issues on that side.
- ✓ **E. Revocation and loss (correct):** access can be withdrawn in the external manager at any time, which makes the data unusable, and the flip side is that lost external keys mean unrecoverable data.

## Key idea
Cloud EKM trades convenience for control: no copy of the key in Google Cloud, revocable access, and the partner's availability becomes your availability.
Q010775:
## Choosing a protection level
Cloud KMS keys have a protection level fixed at creation:
- `SOFTWARE`: operations in software with the BoringCrypto module, FIPS 140-3 Level 1 validated primitives. Cheapest, fine without a hardware requirement.
- `HSM`: Cloud HSM, multi-tenant, FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware, fully managed by Google.
- `HSM_SINGLE_TENANT`: dedicated partitions that the customer administers, giving cryptographic isolation from other customers at extra cost.
- `EXTERNAL` and `EXTERNAL_VPC`: keys held in the customer's external manager.
## Evidence
Each Cloud HSM key has an attestation statement, signed by the HSM hardware with certificates owned by Google and the HSM manufacturer. It can be downloaded with its certificate chains and verified to prove the key attributes and the hardware.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cloud EKM:** this adds an external system and a dependency on its availability that nobody asked for, and attestation evidence for Cloud HSM keys does not come from it.
- ✗ **B. Single-tenant instance:** it adds an instance the company must administer, plus cryptographic isolation and cost that the stem does not require.
- ✗ **C. Software keys:** they are validated at Level 1; a newer standard number does not mean a higher level, and the requirement is Level 3 hardware.
- ✓ **D. Multi-tenant Cloud HSM with attestation (correct):** it meets the FIPS 140-2 Level 3 hardware requirement with no HSM cluster to operate, and the attestation gives per-key proof, which is the evidence the auditor asks for.

## Key idea
Pick the lowest protection level that meets the stated requirement: hardware validation with per-key evidence is Cloud HSM with attestation, not EKM or dedicated HSM unless asked.
Q010776:
## Properties fixed at creation
A key's protection level, purpose and type cannot be changed after creation, and all versions of a key share the protection level. Key material cannot move between storage environments (software, multi-tenant HSM, single-tenant HSM, external). A key and its key ring also cannot be moved to another location.
## What that means for a migration
Moving from software to hardware means a new key with the new protection level, followed by re-protecting what the old key protected. For Cloud Storage the default key of a bucket applies to new objects; existing objects keep their key until they are rewritten.
No principal, including Google, can view or export raw key material, so exporting is not an option.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Delete and recreate by name:** key resources cannot be deleted and recreated like that, and the bucket references a specific key, not a name pattern.
- ✗ **B. New HSM version on the same key:** all versions of a key have the same protection level, so a hardware version cannot be added to a software key.
- ✓ **C. New HSM key, new default, rewrite (correct):** it matches how Cloud KMS works, because the protection level cannot be edited and old objects are re-encrypted only when rewritten with the new key.
- ✗ **D. Export and re-import:** Cloud KMS never exposes raw key material to any principal, and the target would still be a software key.

## Key idea
Protection level is permanent: change it by creating a new key and re-encrypting the data, never by editing the key.
Q010777:
## What rotation does and does not do
Rotating a symmetric key creates a new key version and makes it primary, so new encryption uses it. It does not re-encrypt existing data, and it does not disable or delete older versions. The ciphertext records which version encrypted it, so older versions stay enabled and keep decrypting.
## Responding to a suspected exposure
1. Rotate, so new data uses a fresh version.
2. Re-encrypt existing data under the new primary version.
3. Confirm nothing still depends on the old version, then disable it and schedule it for destruction. A disabled version can be re-enabled; a scheduled one can be restored during the destruction period; a destroyed one cannot be recovered.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Re-encrypt, then retire the old version (correct):** it is the only sequence that removes the exposed material from use, since rotation alone leaves the old version decrypting existing ciphertext.
- ✗ **B. Versions expire:** key versions stay enabled until someone disables or destroys them; the rotation period only decides when the next version is created.
- ✗ **C. Rotate the key ring:** key rings are only containers; rotation happens per key, and nothing re-keys data inside a ring.
- ✗ **D. Delete the key:** keys and key rings cannot be deleted, and Cloud KMS never regenerates and re-encrypts data for you.

## Key idea
Rotation is only the first step of recovery; re-encrypt data and retire the old version to end its usefulness.
Q010778:
## Rotation is different for asymmetric keys
Cloud KMS does not support automatic rotation for asymmetric keys, because additional steps are required before a new version can be used:
- For signing keys, you must distribute the public key of the new version to verifiers, then call the signing method with the new version.
- Asymmetric keys have no primary version; every call names the version to use.
- The purpose and type of a key cannot be changed after creation.
## A safe procedure
Create the version, distribute its public key, switch signing to it, keep the old version enabled long enough for signatures that must still be verified, then disable it. This can be scripted in the pipeline on the required cadence.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Convert to symmetric:** key purpose and type cannot be changed, and a shared symmetric key cannot provide public verification for devices.
- ✓ **B. New version with public key distribution (correct):** it follows the documented asymmetric procedure, allows a staged switch without invalidating devices, and keeps the policy cadence through a scheduled job.
- ✗ **C. Exempt from rotation:** the policy says to replace keys, and the documentation recommends rotation including manual rotation for suspected compromise or algorithm changes.
- ✗ **D. Destroy and fall back:** asymmetric keys have no primary version to fall back to, and destroying the only signing version stops signing.

## Key idea
Asymmetric keys rotate by procedure, not by schedule: create a version, distribute the public key, switch, then retire the old version.
Q010779:
## Key version states
- `ENABLED` can be used. `DISABLED` cannot be used but can be re-enabled.
- `DESTROY_SCHEDULED` cannot be used; the version can be restored to disabled during the destruction period. By default this lasts 30 days.
- `DESTROYED`: key material is gone; ciphertext made with it is not recoverable.
## Tuning the window
The `destroy_scheduled_duration` of a key can be set only when the key is created and cannot be changed afterwards. It applies to all future versions. The range is 24 hours to 120 days, and Google recommends 30 days unless there is a specific requirement. Destroying all versions of a tenant key is a crypto-shredding way to delete that tenant's data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Change later:** the duration is configurable only at creation and cannot be changed, so existing 30-day keys cannot be shortened.
- ✗ **B. Delete key ring:** key rings and keys cannot be deleted, so there is no such shortcut; only versions are destroyed.
- ✓ **C. Short duration set at creation (correct):** three or so days keeps a small recovery window and finishes inside the 7-day commitment, and per-tenant keys make shredding precise.
- ✗ **D. Disable:** a disabled version stays available for re-enabling and is never destroyed automatically.

## Key idea
Set the destruction window when a key is created; crypto-shredding with a per-tenant key then has a predictable, short recovery period.
Q010780:
## CMEK keys as a kill switch
With CMEK the service can operate only while it can use the key. For Cloud SQL, if the instance cannot access the key (for example the key version is disabled), Cloud SQL suspends the instance. When the key is accessible again, Cloud SQL resumes it automatically; the documentation says this can take up to ten minutes for internal validation.
## Related behaviour
- Revoking access of the Cloud SQL service agent also suspends the instance.
- Destroying the key version makes data permanently unrecoverable, which is the deliberate "delete forever" route.
- Enhanced backups also depend on key access: a disabled version blocks restore until it is re-enabled, a destroyed one makes the backup unrestorable.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Data deleted:** disabling a key version is reversible, and no data files are removed.
- ✗ **B. Fallback to Google-managed keys:** Cloud SQL never silently downgrades; that would defeat the purpose of controlling the key.
- ✗ **C. Cloud KMS Admin to the agent:** the problem is the disabled version, not a missing binding, and the admin role manages keys but is not what the service agent needs to use them.
- ✓ **D. Suspend and automatic resume (correct):** the instance is suspended as designed when the key is unusable, and enabling the key version brings it back without data loss.

## Key idea
Disabling a CMEK key version suspends the service that depends on it; re-enable it to resume, and destroy it only to erase data on purpose.
Q010781:
## How key import works
1. Create a target key (a key ring and key whose location and protection level you choose). Skip creating an initial version if you want your material to be version 1.
2. Create an import job with a protection level and an import method (RSA 3072 or 4096-bit wrapping key). The job starts in `PENDING_GENERATION` and must be `ACTIVE` to be used.
3. Wrap your key locally with the import job's public key (automatically by tooling or manually) and send it. The key version is in `PENDING_IMPORT` until it becomes enabled, or `IMPORT_FAILED` if it fails.
## Properties to remember
- An import job expires after three days; create a new one if it lapses.
- Protection level can't be changed after import, and key material cannot be moved between software, HSM and external storage. Location is also fixed.
- Imported keys have automatic rotation disabled by default, and if you enable it, new versions are generated in Cloud KMS.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Existing version blocks import:** importing adds a new version to the target key and has no effect on its existing versions.
- ✗ **B. Export:** no principal can view or export raw key material from Cloud KMS, including through support.
- ✗ **C. Automatic 90-day rotation:** automatic rotation is disabled for imported keys by default, and any new version generated by rotation would be created in Cloud KMS, not on-premises.
- ✓ **D. Fixed protection level (correct):** the import job decides software, HSM or single-tenant HSM, and material stays in that environment, so there is no return trip.
- ✓ **E. Wrapped with an import job (correct):** the key leaves the on-premises HSM protected by the job's wrapping key, and the three-day expiry means a replacement job is needed after that.

## Key idea
Import is a wrapped, time-limited transfer into a fixed protection level; it adds a version and never lets material come back out.
Q010782:
## Keeping Google out of key generation
For imported keys you create the target key without an initial version, and the `import-only` setting stops Cloud KMS from generating key material for any new version; every version must then be imported through an import job. Automatic rotation of imported keys is disabled by default, because enabling it makes Cloud KMS generate new versions itself.
## Rotation of imported keys
Rotation is then a manual or scripted process: generate the new material on-premises, wrap it, import it as a new version, make it primary where needed, re-encrypt data, and retire the old version.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Automatic rotation:** rotation creates versions generated in Cloud KMS, and it cannot pull material from an on-premises HSM.
- ✗ **B. Google-generated first version:** a version generated by Cloud KMS existed, even if destroyed later, which breaks the rule that Google never generates the material.
- ✓ **C. Import-only key with imported versions (correct):** no Google-generated material ever exists, each quarterly version comes from the bank's HSM, and the rotation cadence is run by the bank.
- ✗ **D. Autokey:** Autokey creates its own keys (Cloud HSM, AES-256 GCM, one-year rotation by default) and does not take customer-supplied material.

## Key idea
To keep key origin on-premises, use import-only keys and import each new version; automatic rotation would introduce Cloud KMS-generated material.
Q010783:
## Where IAM and lifecycle attach in Cloud KMS
The hierarchy is project, location, key ring, key, key version. IAM can be set on the project, key ring and key, but not on a key version: granting access to a key grants access to all its enabled versions. Key versions are also what rotation creates over time, so they represent time, not tenants.
Cloud KMS resources can't be moved to a different location after creation, and keys and key rings cannot be deleted; lifecycle actions (disable, destroy) apply to versions or to the entire key.
## Design consequence
If tenants need independent access control and independent erasure, each needs its own key. A shared key ring is fine for grouping, because IAM on each key can differ.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. One key per tenant (correct):** IAM on each key limits who can use that tenant's key, and destroying that key's versions shreds only that tenant's data.
- ✗ **B. Asymmetric keys:** asymmetric versions also share the key's IAM, and the key type does not change who can be granted access.
- ✗ **C. Disable the key ring:** key rings are containers without a state of their own, and the single key would still contain all tenants.
- ✗ **D. IAM Conditions on versions:** access to a key version cannot be managed independently, so there is nothing to attach the condition to.

## Key idea
IAM and destruction scope to a key, not to a version, so isolate tenants with separate keys.
Q010784:
## What Autokey does
Cloud KMS Autokey automates provisioning and assignment of CMEK. When a developer creates a supported resource, the Autokey service agent creates the key ring and key on demand (a key ring called `autokey`, in the dedicated key project or in the resource project for same-project key storage), creates the per-project, per-service service account and grants it encrypt and decrypt on the key.
## Attributes of the keys
- Protection level HSM (multi-tenant Cloud HSM), AES-256 GCM, one-year rotation period by default that an administrator can edit.
- Location: the same location as the resource to be protected; granularity (one key per resource, or per type and location) depends on the service.
- Separation of duties: developers can only request key creation and assignment, administrators manage keys but get no encrypt or decrypt permission.
Like every Cloud KMS key, the protection level cannot be changed later and the key cannot be exported.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Switch to software:** protection level is fixed at creation for every Cloud KMS key, and Autokey keys are HSM keys.
- ✓ **B. Location and HSM (correct):** Autokey creates keys where the resource lives and only in locations where Cloud HSM is available, so other locations need a manually created CMEK.
- ✗ **C. Developers as Cloud KMS Admin:** developers can only request key creation and assignment and cannot view or manage the keys; the Autokey service agent holds the elevated rights.
- ✗ **D. Global key ring:** keys follow the location of each resource and the granularity of the service, so a global reusable key does not exist.
- ✓ **E. Administrators without data access (correct):** they keep full management over the keys but are not given encrypt and decrypt permissions, which preserves separation of duties.

## Key idea
Autokey keys are Cloud HSM, location-matched, and managed by administrators who cannot use them, while developers only request them.
Q010785:
## Default encryption versus CMEK
Google Cloud encrypts customer content at rest by default using envelope encryption: data encryption keys wrapped by key encryption keys in Google's internal key management service. No configuration is needed.
With customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) the key encryption key is a Cloud KMS key you control (software, HSM or external). You choose the location and rotation, see key operations in audit logs, and can disable or destroy key versions to cut off use of the data.
## What CMEK does not do
It does not add encryption that was missing, does not encrypt transport (TLS does), and does not stop an authorized principal who is allowed to read through the service, because the service decrypts on the caller's behalf.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Stopping authorized readers:** services decrypt for principals who have IAM access, so this needs IAM, policy tags or masking, not CMEK.
- ✗ **B. Transit protection:** TLS secures connections; CMEK is a data-at-rest control.
- ✗ **C. Encryption at all:** Cloud Storage and BigQuery encrypt at rest by default, so this is not a reason for CMEK.
- ✓ **D. Control and audit (correct):** CMEK moves rotation, location and key-use logging under the company's governance, which Google-managed keys do not offer.
- ✓ **E. Kill switch (correct):** disabling or destroying the key under company control makes the protected data unusable, a requirement that default encryption cannot satisfy.

## Key idea
Choose CMEK for control, audit and a revocation switch over keys; the default already encrypts, and CMEK does not replace access control.
Q010786:
## Authorized views
A view runs with the view's access to the source, not the caller's. An authorized view lets principals query a subset of data without having access to the source dataset: you put the view in a separate dataset, grant analysts Data Viewer on that dataset, and add the view to the source dataset's authorized views list. The source dataset and the view's dataset must be in the same regional location.
Without authorization, BigQuery checks the caller's own permission on the underlying table, so the query fails with access denied.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Fine-Grained Reader:** this role is for column-level policy tags and has nothing to do with a view reading across datasets.
- ✗ **B. Move the view:** a view in the source dataset would require analysts to have access to that dataset, which loses the separation.
- ✓ **C. Authorize the view (correct):** it gives the view itself access to the source, so analysts see only the exposed columns and never receive permissions on raw_claims.
- ✗ **D. Data Viewer on raw_claims:** this would solve the error but give analysts direct access to the unfiltered table, which they must not have.

## Key idea
Authorized views separate who can query from who can read the source: place the view in its own dataset and authorize it on the source dataset.
Q010787:
## Scope the data role, keep the job role broad
Running a query needs permission to create jobs (BigQuery Job User, `roles/bigquery.jobUser`, on the project that runs the job) and permission to read data on the tables involved. Data Viewer granted on a dataset covers its tables and views; granted on the project it covers every dataset, now and future.
Least privilege therefore puts the data role at dataset (or table) level and only the job-running role at project level.
## Why other fixes fall short
Row-level policies and BigQuery User do not remove the inherited read access to tables, and moving datasets across folders does not change project-level IAM, because datasets stay in the same project.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Move to a folder:** datasets live inside projects; moving a project or dataset elsewhere doesn't drop the grant on the project that still contains it.
- ✓ **B. Dataset-level Data Viewer plus Job User (correct):** it removes the inherited read on payroll and keeps what analysts need to run queries on the two curated datasets.
- ✗ **C. Row access policies:** they must be created on every payroll table now and in future, and tables without a policy stay readable, so this does not remove the standing over-grant.
- ✗ **D. BigQuery User:** it is a project-level role for running jobs and creating datasets; it does not grant dataset reads, so the analysts would still need the dataset grants.

## Key idea
Grant BigQuery data roles on datasets, not projects, and keep only job-running permission at project level.
Q010788:
## Authorized datasets
An authorized dataset lets all views in a dataset access a second dataset. You grant once on the shared (source) dataset; later views added to the authorized dataset can read the source without more edits. Principals get access only to the dataset with the views, or to individual views, and not to the source data.
## Trade-offs
- Granting once also means that any view later created in the authorized dataset can read the source, so control who can create views there.
- Copies avoid the grant but create stale and duplicated sensitive data that needs its own governance.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Authorized dataset (correct):** one grant per source dataset covers all current and future views, and analysts remain locked out of the source tables.
- ✗ **B. Source Data Viewer:** it exposes unfiltered source tables to analysts, which the requirement forbids.
- ✗ **C. Per-view authorization:** it keeps the operational burden the team wants to remove and adds a manual register that can drift from reality.
- ✗ **D. Nightly copies:** they duplicate sensitive data, go stale between refreshes, and add pipelines and storage without improving access control.

## Key idea
Use an authorized dataset to grant once for many views; limit who can create views in it.
Q010789:
## Choose the narrowest object role
Cloud Storage predefined roles differ in object permissions:
- Storage Object Creator (`roles/storage.objectCreator`): create objects only; no view, delete or overwrite.
- Storage Object Viewer: read objects and metadata.
- Storage Object User: create, overwrite, delete and read objects.
- Storage Object Admin and Storage Admin: full control.
Legacy bucket roles carry object permissions too, so they can break least privilege.
## Defense in depth
Pair the grant with object versioning, soft delete or a retention policy, so that even with broader roles an overwritten or deleted object can be recovered.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Viewer plus legacy writer:** the viewer role allows reading, and the legacy writer role includes delete, so both requirements are broken.
- ✗ **B. Storage Admin with a prefix condition:** it still has delete and overwrite inside the prefix, and admin rights are far too broad for a writer.
- ✗ **C. Object User:** it includes read, overwrite and delete, so trust is the only control, which fails under credential theft.
- ✓ **D. Storage Object Creator (correct):** it is the role built for write-only ingestion, and a stolen credential can add files but cannot read, replace or remove existing data.

## Key idea
Write-only ingestion maps to Storage Object Creator; pair with versioning or retention to recover from mistakes.
Q010790:
## Two different exposure paths
- **Public exposure**: granting `allUsers` or `allAuthenticatedUsers` makes data readable by anyone. The Cloud Storage public access prevention constraint (`storage.publicAccessPrevention`) blocks such access.
- **External identities**: adding users or groups from other domains or consumer accounts. The `iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains` constraint limits which identities can be added to IAM policies to those in the allowed customer IDs.
## What the other constraints do
Uniform bucket-level access ends ACLs but still allows IAM grants to anyone. Locations and CMEK constraints address residency and key ownership, not who can read.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Public access prevention (correct):** it blocks anonymous and all-authenticated-user access at bucket and project level, closing the public path.
- ✗ **B. Non-CMEK restriction:** it requires customer-managed keys for supported services; encryption does not prevent authorized-looking grants.
- ✗ **C. Resource locations:** it limits where resources are created, not who can read them.
- ✗ **D. Uniform bucket-level access:** it only ensures IAM is the single permission system; an IAM grant to anyone is still possible.
- ✓ **E. Domain restricted sharing (correct):** it stops IAM grants to identities outside the allowed customer IDs, closing the external sharing path.

## Key idea
Combine public access prevention (no anonymous access) with domain restricted sharing (no outside identities) to cover both exposure paths.
Q010791:
## IAM database authentication
Cloud SQL supports two ways to authenticate a database user: built-in (username and password) and IAM database authentication, where an OAuth 2.0 access token proves the identity. A principal needs the Cloud SQL Instance User role (`cloudsql.instanceUser`, which contains `cloudsql.instances.login`) to log in, and the Cloud SQL Client role to connect.
With automatic IAM database authentication, a Cloud SQL connector or the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy requests and refreshes tokens, which are short-lived (valid for one hour). Each service uses its own service account, so logins are attributable and no password is stored.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Authorized network ranges:** IPs say nothing about which workload connected, shared egress ranges are broad, and this is network allow-listing, not authentication.
- ✗ **B. Hourly rotation with a shared user:** passwords still exist, and one shared user hides which workload connected.
- ✓ **C. IAM database authentication with connectors (correct):** no password to leak, short-lived tokens, and logins map to each workload's service account, which meets both goals.
- ✗ **D. Single client certificate:** one certificate shared across services cannot tell workloads apart and is still a long-lived credential.

## Key idea
Use IAM database authentication through a connector to replace passwords with short-lived, per-identity tokens.
Q010792:
## What the constraints do
- `sql.restrictPublicIp` restricts configuring a public IP on Cloud SQL instances where it is enforced.
- `sql.restrictAuthorizedNetworks` restricts adding authorized networks for unproxied access.
Both are boolean constraints and, as the documentation states, are not retroactive: instances that already have a public IP or authorized networks keep working after the constraint is enforced.
## Closing the gap
Use inventory (for example Cloud Asset Inventory or Security Command Center findings) to find existing public instances, move clients to private IP or the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, and then remove the public IP and authorized networks.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Restart:** a restart does not evaluate the constraint; the public IP must be removed by changing the instance configuration.
- ✓ **B. Not retroactive (correct):** guardrails stop new violations but leave old instances, so the old ones must be remediated and verified separately.
- ✗ **C. 30-day delay:** policy changes apply to new configuration right away; no timer applies them to existing instances.
- ✗ **D. Only MySQL:** Cloud SQL constraints apply to the Cloud SQL service, not to one database engine.

## Key idea
Organization policy guardrails prevent new public Cloud SQL exposure but do not repair existing instances; scan and remediate them.
Q010793:
## Global versus regional secrets
- The **global** service stores a secret as a global resource, and replication policies (automatic or user-managed) decide where it is stored. Applications can access it from any region.
- The **regional** service creates secrets in a specific location. The documentation states that the secret data stays within that location at rest, in use and in transit, that regional secrets are not automatically replicated, and that they can be accessed only by applications or services in the same location.
## Choosing
Use regional secrets for strict data residency and sovereignty; use global secrets with automatic replication when residency does not matter.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. VPC Service Controls:** a perimeter limits who can call the API, not where data is stored or processed.
- ✗ **B. CMEK in Frankfurt:** a key protects the content at rest; it does not decide where the secret is served from or used.
- ✗ **C. Resource locations with global secrets:** it controls where replicas can be placed but does not make the service itself regional for processing and transport.
- ✓ **D. Regional secrets (correct):** they are the feature built to keep storage, processing and transport in one location, and they limit access to workloads in that location.

## Key idea
For residency at rest, in use and in transit, choose regional Secret Manager secrets rather than combining controls on global secrets.
Q010794:
## Version handling in Secret Manager
A secret holds versions; the `latest` alias always points to the newest enabled version. Google's best practices say to reference secrets by version number, deploy changes to version numbers through your release process, and disable versions before destroying them, so that you have a reversible state that looks the same as destroyed to consumers.
## Related practices
- Give consumers only Secret Manager Secret Accessor, on a single secret rather than a whole project.
- Avoid environment variables and the file system for secrets where possible.
- Rotate regularly and monitor with Cloud Asset Inventory and data access logs.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Version Manager for the service:** it lets a compromised or buggy consumer change and disable secret versions, which exceeds what a reader needs.
- ✗ **B. Destroy old versions:** destruction is irreversible and removes the rollback path just when it is needed.
- ✓ **C. Pin and stage (correct):** a pinned version cannot change underneath running instances, new versions roll out like code, and disabled versions can be re-enabled if something still depends on them.
- ✗ **D. Build-time copy:** this puts the secret in an image or build output, which expands exposure and breaks rotation.

## Key idea
Pin secret versions in deployments and disable before destroying, so a bad rotation can be rolled back without an outage.
Q010795:
## What a Secret Manager rotation schedule really does
Secret Manager does not change credentials itself. At the secret's `next_rotation_time` (set directly, or computed from a `rotation_period`) it publishes a `SECRET_ROTATE` message to the Pub/Sub topics configured on the secret. You must create a subscriber (for example a Cloud Run function) that receives the message, generates or requests the new credential at the system that issues it, and adds it as a new secret version, and also deploy it to consumers if they pin versions.
The notification can fail to deliver if topic permissions or configuration are wrong, and overlapping rotations are skipped.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Subscriber workflow (correct):** the message is only a trigger; without a consumer that creates the credential and the version, nothing changes, which matches the symptoms.
- ✗ **B. Schedule on versions:** rotation schedules belong to the secret, not to its versions.
- ✗ **C. Remove latest alias:** adding a version is always allowed, and the alias moves to the new version.
- ✗ **D. CMEK required:** rotation notifications do not depend on CMEK.

## Key idea
Secret Manager rotation sends a Pub/Sub notification; your subscriber must perform the rotation and add the version.
Q010796:
## The metadata server and SSRF
Every Compute Engine VM can query its metadata server without extra authorization, and the same server issues access tokens for the VM's attached service account. The documentation warns that any process that can query the metadata URL has access to all its values. Requests need the `Metadata-Flavor: Google` header, but a server-side request forgery (SSRF) bug or a sandbox escape can supply it.
## Layers of defence
- Reduce the value of the token: use a dedicated user-managed service account with minimal roles instead of the default one.
- Reduce reachability: validate and block internal destinations in code, and sandbox components that process untrusted input.
- Metadata traffic never leaves the physical host, so network settings such as Private Google Access do not affect it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Rotate keys:** the token comes from the metadata server and is not derived from a downloaded key, so key rotation changes nothing.
- ✓ **B. Least-privilege service account (correct):** even if the token is stolen, it allows only the application's narrow permissions.
- ✗ **C. Private Google Access:** it controls how VMs without external IPs reach Google APIs and has no effect on the metadata server, which is on the host.
- ✗ **D. OS Login:** it governs SSH access to the VM, not who can call the metadata server from inside.
- ✓ **E. Block and sandbox (correct):** the app stops fetching the metadata endpoints on an attacker's behalf, and a sandboxed fetcher cannot reach the server at all.

## Key idea
Limit what a metadata token can do (dedicated minimal service account) and who can ask for it (block internal destinations, sandbox untrusted parsing).
Q010797:
## Metadata is not a secret store
The metadata server returns every custom value to any process that can reach the metadata URL, and custom metadata (including startup-script text) can be read by principals allowed to view the instance or project metadata. Google recommends caution when writing sensitive values, including client certificates and private keys, to the metadata server.
## Better pattern
Store the secret in Secret Manager, grant Secret Manager Secret Accessor on that secret to the VM's dedicated service account, and fetch the value at boot using the API. Access is then limited per secret, logged in data access logs, and rotatable without changing instance metadata.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Secret Manager with the VM's identity (correct):** the secret is no longer visible to every process and metadata viewer, and each read is authorized and auditable.
- ✗ **B. Unencrypted on disk:** metadata is not stored on the boot disk and encrypting a disk does not change who can read metadata.
- ✗ **C. Shutdown script:** this changes when the script runs but leaves the password in metadata for any process to read.
- ✗ **D. Visible to all projects:** metadata is per instance and project; other projects cannot read it, so the exposure is inside the VM and among viewers.

## Key idea
Do not place secrets in VM metadata; keep them in Secret Manager and fetch them with the VM's own service account.
Q010798:
## OS Login
OS Login ties SSH access to IAM: access comes from roles such as OS Login (`roles/compute.osLogin`) and OS Admin Login, and is audited. When OS Login is enabled on a VM, Compute Engine deletes the VM's `authorized_keys` files and no longer accepts SSH keys stored in project or instance metadata.
The `compute.managed.requireOsLogin` constraint (legacy form `compute.requireOsLogin`) enables OS Login on newly created projects and prevents metadata updates that disable OS Login at project or instance level, turning a convention into a guardrail.
## Why the alternatives are weaker
Per-VM settings depend on discipline, key rotation keeps a shared key model, and removing external IPs does not stop SSH from internal networks, Identity-Aware Proxy or VPN.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Remove external IPs:** SSH keys also work over internal routes, IAP and VPN, so keys in metadata would still grant access.
- ✓ **B. Require OS Login (correct):** it moves SSH to IAM, ignores metadata-stored keys, and prevents turning OS Login off through metadata, so a metadata edit no longer grants login.
- ✗ **C. Daily rotation of a shared key:** one project key still unlocks every VM, and reviewers must catch each change.
- ✗ **D. Manual blocking:** it is per instance, relies on every team, and new VMs can miss it.

## Key idea
Use OS Login enforced by organization policy so SSH access is IAM-based and editing metadata cannot add logins.
Q010799:
## Node identity versus workload identity
By default, pods can reach the node's metadata server and obtain tokens for the node's service account, so every pod shares the node's permissions. Workload Identity Federation for GKE deploys the GKE metadata server on every node (node pools set to `GKE_METADATA` mode). It intercepts credential requests from workloads and answers for the workload's Kubernetes identity instead of the node's, so code that already uses Application Default Credentials keeps working. You then grant IAM roles directly to the Kubernetes service account principals.
## Compare
Namespaces are a Kubernetes boundary, not a credential boundary, keys add long-lived secrets, and widening the node account increases blast radius.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Union of roles on the node account:** every pod inherits all roles, which is the opposite of per-workload least privilege.
- ✗ **B. Keys as Secrets:** long-lived keys are exactly what workload identity avoids, and they can be stolen from the cluster.
- ✗ **C. Namespaces:** they do not block network access to the metadata server or change which identity it returns.
- ✓ **D. Workload Identity Federation for GKE (correct):** the GKE metadata server stops pods from obtaining node credentials and issues per-workload identities with least-privilege IAM roles.

## Key idea
Protect the metadata path on GKE with Workload Identity Federation (GKE metadata server) so pods get their own scoped identity, not the node's.
Q010800:
## Attestors and attestations
Binary Authorization decides at deploy time whether an image may run. A policy has a default rule plus optional specific rules, and each rule has an evaluation mode and an enforcement mode.
- An **attestation** is a record, signed with a private key, that states a specific image digest completed a stage such as QA or security review.
- An **attestor** is the Binary Authorization resource that holds the matching public key and verifies those signatures at deploy time.
- A rule in the require-attestations mode lists one or more attestors.
## Modelling two independent approvals
When several attestors are listed in one rule, the image must have attestations that are verified by all of them. One attestor per approving team therefore gives a logical AND. Each team keeps its own key, so neither can forge the other's approval.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Allow all images with manual cleanup:** allow all images disables deploy-time enforcement, and deleting images after the fact is a slow detective step that lets untested images run first.
- ✗ **B. At-least-one semantics:** listing several attestors does not behave as OR, so this would be a wrong description of the rule and would not guarantee both reviews.
- ✓ **C. Require attestations with both attestors listed (correct):** the policy admits the image only when the QA attestor and the security attestor each verify an attestation, which enforces both approvals with separate keys.
- ✗ **D. Single shared key:** one signature cannot show that two independent teams approved, and either team could sign on behalf of the other, which destroys separation of duties.

## Key idea
Several attestors in one require-attestations rule means every one of them must verify an attestation, which models independent approvals.
Q010801:
## One policy per project, resources elsewhere
Each Google Cloud project can have exactly one Binary Authorization policy, and it must be in the project where the deployment platform runs. Attestors and attestations are separate resources that can live in other projects.
## Separation of duties
In a single-project setup everything is together, so anyone with enough IAM in that project can change the policy and also create the approval. In a **multi-project setup**:
- the deployment project (for example the GKE project) holds only the policy;
- the attestor project holds attestors and the Cloud KMS keys that sign and verify;
- an attestation project holds the attestation records.
IAM is configured separately in each project, so no single role can both create an approval and relax the rule that demands it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Owner for CI in production:** giving the pipeline broad ownership lets one identity edit the policy and sign any image, the opposite of separation of duties.
- ✗ **B. Naming the attestor:** a label does not stop the same identity from signing and administering; it only improves readability of logs.
- ✓ **C. Multi-project configuration (correct):** the policy owner, signing authority and attestation store are different IAM boundaries, so a compromised pipeline identity cannot rewrite the policy or mint approvals outside the roles it was given.
- ✗ **D. Key in a bucket:** a private signing key kept in object storage is exposed to anyone who obtains the service account, whereas Cloud KMS keeps the private key non-exportable and signs on request.

## Key idea
Split policy, attestors and attestations into different projects so no single identity can both approve and relax enforcement.
Q010802:
## Evaluation mode versus enforcement mode
Each rule has two independent settings:
- The **evaluation mode** says what is checked: allow all images, disallow all images, or require attestations.
- The **enforcement mode** says what happens when an image fails: **Block and Audit Log**, or **Dry Run: Audit Log Only**.
## Using dry run to roll out safely
Dry run lets the policy be tested in the real environment before enforcement takes effect. Non-conformant images are allowed, but the deployment details are recorded in Cloud Audit Logs. The team reviews those entries, signs or fixes the offending pipelines, and only then switches to Block and Audit Log. Most production rules use blocking; dry run is for validation.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Disallow everything first:** blocking from day one stops all deployments except exempt images and turns the measurement into an outage.
- ✗ **B. Test only on an empty cluster:** it exercises no real deployment pipelines, so it cannot reveal which production teams deploy unsigned images.
- ✗ **C. Reading node logs:** node pull logs do not record policy decisions or attestation status, so they cannot show what the policy would have blocked.
- ✓ **D. Dry Run (correct):** Audit Log Only: it tests the real policy against real deployments with no outage and produces the Cloud Audit Logs entries needed to find unsigned images.

## Key idea
Roll out a require-attestations rule in Dry Run: Audit Log Only first, read the audit log violations, then enforce with Block and Audit Log.
Q010803:
## Break-glass
Break-glass is an emergency escape hatch that lets a team deploy an image that Binary Authorization would block. It is consistent with the Kubernetes admission controller specification.
- It is requested per Pod by adding the break-glass label to the Pod specification.
- A **break-glass event** is automatically logged to Cloud Audit Logs, whether or not the image satisfied the policy.
## Governing the exception
Because the request is just a label on the Pod, Kubernetes RBAC on who may create Pods decides who can use it. The audit entries give the security team something to review or to wire to an alert.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Cloud Audit Logs entry (correct):** each use is logged automatically, and the entries can be audited or used to trigger alerts and downstream actions.
- ✗ **B. Permanent exemption:** the label affects only that deployment; it does not add the image to the exempt list or create attestations.
- ✗ **C. Logging only violations:** the event is logged regardless of whether the image would have satisfied the policy.
- ✗ **D. Second weekend policy:** break-glass is a per-Pod override, not a second policy, and a project has exactly one policy.
- ✓ **E. Label on the Pod specification (correct):** break-glass is requested in the workload itself, so Pod creation rights govern who can invoke it.

## Key idea
Break-glass is a Pod label that overrides enforcement for one deployment and is always written to Cloud Audit Logs.
Q010804:
## Exempt images and system images
A policy's rules apply to every image that is not exempt. Two mechanisms keep a strict default rule from blocking the cluster itself:
- **Exempt images**: an allowlist of registry paths (`admissionWhitelistPatterns`) that Binary Authorization always allows. Paths such as `gcr.io/google_containers/*` and `k8s.gcr.io/**` are exempt by default because GKE needs them to start a cluster.
- **Trust Google-maintained system images**: set with `globalPolicyEvaluationMode`; a Google-managed system policy is evaluated before and in addition to the user policy, so images GKE requires are not blocked.
## Fix
Turn on the system-image trust and keep the strict default for everything else.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Allow all by default:** this flips the model from deny-by-default to allow-by-default, so any unsigned application image would be admitted unless a rule catches it.
- ✓ **B. Trust Google-maintained system images (correct):** Google's list of required system images is exempted without the team maintaining paths, and the strict default rule still blocks any other image.
- ✗ **C. Permanent dry run:** dry run stops all blocking, and the claim that system images cannot be evaluated is wrong; they are handled by exemption.
- ✗ **D. Deleting the policy:** removing the policy disables enforcement entirely, and node auto-upgrade does not evaluate image provenance.

## Key idea
Pair a deny-by-default rule with the Google-maintained system images trust (or exempt paths) so GKE can start while everything else is blocked.
Q010805:
## Binary Authorization on Cloud Run
Cloud Run supports Binary Authorization policy for services and jobs. Differences from GKE:
- Only the **default rule** is supported; specific rules (cluster, namespace, service account) are not available for Cloud Run.
- The policy is read from the project where the service runs.
## Requiring it centrally
An organization policy constraint, `run.allowedBinaryAuthorizationPolicies`, can be set on an organization, folder or project to require enforcement. Allowing only the custom value `default` tells Cloud Run to use the Binary Authorization policy in the same project as the service. Because organization policies are inherited, individual teams cannot omit it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Organization policy allowing only default (correct):** it forces every Cloud Run deployment in scope to use the project's own policy and cannot be skipped per service.
- ✗ **B. Admission webhook:** Cloud Run is fully managed and has no Kubernetes admission webhook configuration; enforcement is a platform integration.
- ✗ **C. Per-deployment flag with quarterly review:** it relies on each team remembering the flag, and violations stay undetected for months.
- ✗ **D. Specific rules for Cloud Run:** Cloud Run supports only the default rule, so there are no cluster or service specific rules to create.

## Key idea
Require Binary Authorization on Cloud Run with an organization policy constraint set to the value default; Cloud Run supports only the default rule.
Q010806:
## What an attestation is bound to
An attestation is a signed record that contains the image's registry path and digest. The digest is the content hash of the image, so identical bytes have an identical digest wherever they are stored.
## Promoting between registries
Binary Authorization documentation states that a single attestation can authorize identical images stored in multiple locations or registries (Artifact Registry, Container Registry, or an external registry). A promotion pipeline that copies by digest can reuse the attestation, which also means the promoted image is provably the one that was approved. Deploying a rebuilt image would create a new digest and need a new attestation.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Expiry on copy:** attestations are stored in the attestation project as metadata, not in the repository, and are not removed when an image is copied.
- ✓ **B. Digest-bound attestation (correct):** identical images in different registries share a digest, so one attestation covers the staging copy and the promoted copy.
- ✗ **C. Path-bound attestation:** the signed content includes the digest, and the documentation says one attestation can authorize identical images across registries.
- ✗ **D. Only Artifact Registry images:** images in Container Registry and external registries are supported, so no rebuild is needed.

## Key idea
Attestations bind to the image digest, so one attestation can cover the same image in several registries.
Q010807:
## Deploy-time versus ongoing checks
Binary Authorization has two roles in the overview documentation:
- **Enforce**: images being deployed to a supported platform are checked against policy, then allowed or blocked. The overview describes this as a one-time image validation at deploy time.
- **Monitor**: **continuous validation (CV)** periodically checks the metadata of images associated with running Pods for continued conformance and logs violations to Cloud Logging.
## Status to remember
The check-based platform policy form of CV is marked Preview in the current documentation, so a production design should not depend on it being generally available; combine deploy-time enforcement with vulnerability monitoring and posture findings.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Build-time only:** enforcement happens at deployment on the target platform, not inside Cloud Build.
- ✗ **B. Platform difference:** neither platform is continuously enforced by the deploy-time check, and Cloud Run uses the same policy model with only a default rule.
- ✗ **C. Automatic re-evaluation and eviction:** enforcement does not evict running Pods when the policy changes; that is not how the admission-time check works.
- ✓ **D. One-time enforcement versus separate monitoring (correct):** enforcement decides at deployment, and ongoing conformance checks of running Pods are the job of continuous validation.

## Key idea
Binary Authorization enforcement is a deploy-time gate; monitoring running Pods is the separate (check-based, currently Preview) continuous validation feature.
Q010808:
## Trusted image policies
The constraint `compute.trustedImageProjects` is an organization policy that defines which projects' images principals may use to create persistent disks. It can be set on a project, folder or organization and is inherited.
## What it does not do
Documented limitations:
- Custom images in the **local project** are not restricted.
- Image files in **Cloud Storage buckets** are not restricted.
- Users are not prevented from **creating image resources** in their local projects.
So the constraint governs where approved images come from, but a developer who can create images in their own project can still use them. Closing that gap needs IAM that limits image creation, plus detection of images outside the golden project.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Blocks image creation:** the documentation states trusted image policies do not prevent users from creating images in their local projects.
- ✗ **B. Scans Cloud Storage images:** image files in buckets are listed as not restricted, and the constraint does not scan contents.
- ✓ **C. Local-project gap (correct):** custom images in the developer's own project are not covered, so they remain usable unless image creation rights are restricted.
- ✗ **D. Project-only scope:** it can be set on a project, folder or organization and inherits down.
- ✓ **E. Restricts image sources (correct):** setting the constraint at organization scope limits disk creation to images from the listed projects.

## Key idea
compute.trustedImageProjects limits image sources org-wide but leaves local-project custom images and Cloud Storage image files uncovered.
Q010809:
## Predefined posture templates
The security posture service ships predefined templates that follow a compliance standard (for example CIS, NIST SP 800-53, ISO 27001, PCI DSS) or a Google-recommended standard. Two naming patterns matter:
- **Essentials** templates can be deployed without changes.
- **Extended** templates must be customized to match the environment before they are deployed.
A posture is built from policy sets, and its policies can be preventative (organization policy constraints) or detective (Security Health Analytics detectors). The service needs Security Command Center Premium or Enterprise activated at the organization level; this question does not depend on tier.
## Why customize
Extended templates carry settings that depend on the environment, so deploying them as shipped would not reflect the organization's own requirements.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Binary Authorization conversion:** a posture is made of organization policy and Security Health Analytics policies, not image attestations.
- ✗ **B. Deploy any template unchanged:** only some templates are documented as deployable without changes; extended ones are not, and findings are not an editing surface.
- ✗ **C. Detective policies removed:** postures may contain detective policies such as Security Health Analytics detectors alongside preventative constraints.
- ✓ **D. Customize before deploying (correct):** the documentation states that an extended template must be customized to the environment before deployment, whereas an essentials template can be used unchanged.

## Key idea
Essentials posture templates deploy as shipped; extended templates must be customized to the environment first.
Q010810:
## Default rule and specific rules
A Binary Authorization policy has one **default rule** and optional **specific rules**. The default rule applies to every non-exempt image that has no more specific rule. On GKE, specific rules can target clusters, Kubernetes namespaces and Kubernetes service accounts; in the policy file a cluster-specific rule sits in a `clusterAdmissionRule` node.
- Each project has exactly one policy, so per-cluster behaviour comes from rules inside that policy, not from extra policies.
- A strict default means a cluster added later is protected until a specific rule relaxes it.
## Applying it here
Put the strict requirement (require attestations, QA attestor) in the default rule and relax only the development cluster with a specific rule set to allow all images. The relaxation is explicit and visible in the policy.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Break-glass on every Pod:** break-glass is an emergency override that is audited each time, so using it as the normal development path floods the audit log and makes real emergencies hard to spot.
- ✗ **B. One policy per cluster:** the policy is a per-project resource shared by all its clusters, and the default rule always exists.
- ✓ **C. Strict default plus a development cluster rule (correct):** production and any future cluster inherit the attestation requirement, and only the named development cluster is relaxed.
- ✗ **D. Allow-all default with a second policy:** a project can have only one policy, and an allow-all default would leave every new cluster unprotected.

## Key idea
Use a strict default rule and relax individual GKE clusters with cluster-specific rules inside the project's single policy.
Q010811:
## Reboot options in patch jobs
A patch job installs updates through the VM's package manager, and some updates (a new kernel is the typical case) only take effect after a restart. The patch job has three reboot options:
- **Default**: the agent checks well-known signals on each OS and decides whether a reboot is needed.
- **Always**: the machine reboots after the update completes.
- **Never**: no reboot; in some cases this means not all patches are fully applied.
## Maintenance window
The maintenance window is the time allowed for the job; no new patch work starts after it ends. It limits when patching happens, not what is running afterwards. Schedule the window when a restart is acceptable, or use rolling replacement for stateless groups.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Reboot Always or Default (correct):** the restart is what activates the installed kernel, and the maintenance window keeps the disruption in an agreed period.
- ✗ **B. Longer window:** the window only bounds how long patching may run; success does not mean the new kernel is active.
- ✗ **C. Second update run:** running the update again installs nothing new, and a kernel in use is replaced only by a restart.
- ✗ **D. Reinstalling the agent:** the agent already applied the updates through the package manager; the missing step is the restart.

## Key idea
Reboot option Never can leave patches not fully applied; use Default or Always inside a maintenance window.
Q010812:
## Security posture service
Security Command Center includes a **security posture service** to define, deploy and monitor a security posture. It requires the Premium or Enterprise tier with SCC activated at the organization level.
- A **posture** is one or more **policy sets**; each holds **policies**: preventative (organization policy constraints, including custom constraints) or detective (Security Health Analytics detectors, including custom modules).
- A posture is **deployed** at an organization, folder or project; only one posture can be deployed to each resource.
- Postures are **inherited**. If a lower-level posture defines a policy differently (Allow versus Deny), the lower-level definition is used by resources below it. Google recommends a broad organization posture with stricter ones on folders and projects.
- After deployment, **drift** (an unauthorized change from the posture) is reported as SCC findings, which can be reviewed, filtered and exported.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Binary Authorization policy:** it governs container image deployment on supported platforms, not general resource configuration or drift.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Security posture service with org-level and folder-level postures: it bundles preventative and detective policies, supports hierarchical inheritance and reports drift as findings.
- ✗ **C. Standard tier alone:** the posture service is not available without Premium or Enterprise, and predefined detectors cannot enforce organization policy constraints.
- ✗ **D. Asset Inventory plus hand-built queries:** it can detect differences but the team must build and maintain the comparison and has no deployable preventative policies.

## Key idea
Use SCC security postures: bundle org policy constraints and SHA detectors, deploy hierarchically, and watch drift findings.
Q010813:
## Components and behaviours
- **Policies** are either preventative (organization policy constraints) or detective (SHA detectors, including custom modules and custom constraints).
